name: Valse à deux temps

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A dance historian specializing in 19th-century ballroom etiquette.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Russian Waltz that Conquered Paris
This is Valse à deux temps. 19th century.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: Valse à deux temps · France · 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in Russia and was introduced to Paris in 1839 by the Baron de Nieuken, who learned the steps from a professor while preparing for a ball given by Count Mole.
on_screen: Map: France · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It served as a social ballroom dance, favored by the Russian delegation and later adopted by Parisian society for its energetic and novel rhythmic interpretation.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers execute a slide to the side on the first beat, bend the knees slightly on the second beat, and bring the trailing foot behind the leading foot on the third beat.
The movement is performed on a diagonal path.
Watch for Two-step sequence.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Diagonal movement forward and backward.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to three-beat waltz music, though the dancers interpret the measure as two distinct movements rather than three.
The pulse is 3/4.
Standard waltz music in 3/4 time, but interpreted by the dancers as a two-beat rhythm.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Verified recording — MISSING

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Baron de Nieuken, the Prince of Galitzine, the Count of Damas, and the Marquis de La Baume were among the first practitioners in Paris.
A simplified version was created at the public ballroom La Chaumière, where dancers jumped on alternating feet without strict adherence to the music.
The dance is a variant of the traditional three-beat waltz.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Valse à deux temps (France). Meter 3/4. Rhythm pattern: Two movements per three-beat measure.. Mood: energetic, brio. It should sound like this: Standard waltz music in 3/4 time, but interpreted by the dancers as a two-beat rhythm.
